tagline: Paul's longest and most carefully argued letter: the gospel of God's righteousness, for Jew and Gentile alike, set out for a church he had never visited.
overview:
Romans is a letter, but it reads at times like a sustained argument. Paul wrote it to the Christians in Rome, a mixed community of Jewish and Gentile believers whom he had not yet met, to introduce himself and the gospel he preached before he arrived. He states his theme early: the gospel “is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (1:16), because in it “the righteousness of God” is revealed (1:17). The rest of the letter works that sentence out.

The argument moves in large blocks. Paul first shows that the whole human race, Gentile and Jew, stands guilty before God (1:18-3:20). He then announces that God has acted in Jesus Christ to put people right with himself as a gift received by faith, and shows that Abraham was counted righteous in exactly that way (3:21-4:25). He describes the new life that follows: peace with God, freedom from the reign of sin and death, the struggle with the law, and life in the Spirit that ends in the renewal of all creation (chapters 5 to 8). He wrestles openly with the painful question of why most of his own people, Israel, have not believed (chapters 9 to 11). Finally he turns to how a people saved by mercy should live together, especially when Jewish and Gentile believers disagree over food and holy days (12:1-15:13), and closes with his travel plans and a long list of greetings.

Romans stands behind turning points in the lives of Augustine, Martin Luther, and John Wesley, and behind the Protestant Reformation's teaching on justification by faith. It remains at the center of debate today about what Paul meant by the law, by works, and by righteousness. A first-time reader will find it demanding, but its questions are the deepest ones: what is wrong with us, what God has done about it, and what kind of people that makes us.
author:
The letter names Paul as its author (1:1), and this is one of the few points in New Testament scholarship on which virtually everyone agrees. Romans belongs with Galatians and the Corinthian letters as the core of the undisputed Pauline letters, and even the most skeptical critical traditions have accepted it as his. Paul dictated it: a man named Tertius, who actually wrote it down, adds his own greeting near the end (16:22), which was common practice for letters in the Roman world.

The debates concern the letter's form rather than its author. Early manuscripts show that Romans circulated in more than one form, and the closing doxology (16:25-27) appears at different places in different manuscripts. Some scholars have argued that chapter 16, with its many greetings to named people, was originally a separate note sent to Ephesus, since Paul seems to know a surprising number of people in a city he had never visited. Most scholars today hold that chapter 16 belongs to the letter to Rome, noting that travel between Rome and the eastern cities was frequent and that Paul had good reason to greet every acquaintance he had in a church where he hoped to be welcomed.
date: Romans is usually dated to about AD 57, with a range of roughly AD 55 to 58, and it was most likely written from Corinth in Greece. The evidence fits together well. Paul says he is about to take a collection from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor believers in Jerusalem (15:25-26), which matches the end of his third missionary campaign. Acts reports that he then spent three months in Greece before that trip to Jerusalem (Acts 20:2-3). The letter commends Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth, who probably carried it (16:1-2), and it sends greetings from Gaius, Paul's host (16:23), likely the Gaius Paul baptized in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14). The exact year depends on how one reconstructs Paul's chronology, but the setting is widely agreed.
setting:
Rome in the 50s AD was the capital of an empire that ran from Spain to Syria, a crowded city of perhaps a million people drawn from every province. It had a large Jewish community, with many synagogues, and the gospel almost certainly reached Rome through Jewish believers who had traveled there, well before any apostle arrived. Nobody knows who first founded the church; Paul himself never claims it, and he says he has not yet visited (1:13).

An event under the emperor Claudius shaped the church Paul addressed. The Roman historian Suetonius reports that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because of constant disturbances at the instigation of one Chrestus, which many scholars take as a garbled reference to disputes about Christ. Acts mentions the same expulsion: Aquila and Priscilla had come to Corinth from Italy because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2). The edict is usually dated to about AD 49, though some date it earlier. For several years the Roman church would have been led largely by Gentile believers. After Claudius died in AD 54, Jews were able to return (Priscilla and Aquila are back in Rome in Romans 16:3), and a church that had grown in a Gentile direction now had to welcome back Jewish believers with their own convictions about food, the Sabbath, and the law. Many interpreters read the letter's concern for Jew and Gentile together, and its long appeal for mutual acceptance in chapters 14 and 15, against that background.
purpose:
Paul gives some of his reasons himself. He had long wanted to visit Rome (1:10-15). He was about to go to Jerusalem with the collection, and he was anxious about how he would be received there (15:30-31). After that he planned to go on to Spain and hoped the Roman church would help send him (15:24, 28). The letter introduces him and his gospel to a church whose support he needed, and it answers suspicions that his preaching of grace made the law worthless or encouraged sin (3:8, 6:1).

Beyond those practical aims, scholars weigh how much of the letter addresses tensions inside the Roman church itself. Some read Romans chiefly as a summary of Paul's gospel, prepared at a turning point in his work. Others stress that its long treatment of Jew and Gentile, of Israel's future, and of the strong and the weak addresses a divided congregation that needed to hear that God's mercy had made them one people. Most see both aims at work.
story: Romans comes after the Gospels and Acts in the Christian Bible and opens the collection of Paul's letters. Historically it belongs inside the story of Acts: Paul wrote it during the three months in Greece described in Acts 20:2-3, just before the trip to Jerusalem where he was arrested (Acts 21). When Acts closes with Paul finally in Rome, under guard, the church there already has this letter in its hands. Romans also looks back across the whole Old Testament, drawing on Genesis, the Psalms, Isaiah, and the prophets more heavily than any other Pauline letter, to argue that the gospel is not a new religion but the fulfillment of what God promised Abraham and spoke through the prophets.
christ: Romans opens by defining the gospel as the message about God's Son, descended from David according to the flesh and declared Son of God with power by his resurrection from the dead (1:3-4). Everything in the letter hangs on that person and what he has done. Christ's death is the place where God displays his righteousness and deals with sin (3:21-26). He is the second Adam, whose obedience undoes the ruin that came through the first (5:12-21). Believers are united with him in his death and resurrection (chapter 6), are free from condemnation because they are in him (8:1), and share his inheritance as God's children (8:17). He is the goal of the law (10:4), the one Israel's Scriptures promised, and the Lord whom Jew and Gentile call on alike (10:12-13). Romans is not a treatise on salvation in the abstract. It is a letter about what God has done in Jesus.
reading:
Read Romans as an argument, and follow the conversation. Paul often raises an objection in the voice of an imagined opponent and answers it, a style ancient teachers called the diatribe, so a question such as “What then shall we say?” usually signals a turn. Read whole sections before stopping on single verses, since many famous verses mean more inside their paragraph than on a poster. Notice how often Paul quotes the Old Testament and pay attention to the passages he quotes.

The first common misreading treats Romans as only about how an individual gets to heaven, missing its concern for how Jews and Gentiles become one people under God. The second swings the other way and treats it only as a letter about ethnic groups, missing its searching treatment of sin, guilt, and grace for every person. Paul means both. It also rewards patience: chapters 9 to 11 are not a detour but the place where Paul asks whether God has kept his promises, which is the question the whole letter depends on.

structure.title: Greeting and theme
structure.summary: Paul introduces himself, his gospel about God's Son, and his long-delayed plan to visit Rome, then states the letter's theme: the gospel is God's power for salvation, revealing his righteousness by faith.

structure.title: The whole world under sin
structure.summary: Gentiles who suppressed what they knew of God, and Jews who had the law and did not keep it, stand together before God's judgment. No one is declared righteous by works of the law.

structure.title: Righteousness through faith
structure.summary: God has revealed his righteousness apart from the law through faith in Jesus Christ (or, as some read the Greek, the faithfulness of Jesus Christ), whose death is the place of atonement. Abraham, counted righteous by faith before circumcision, is the father of all who believe.

structure.title: New life and sure hope
structure.summary: Justified believers have peace with God. Christ undoes Adam's ruin, believers die and rise with him, the law's role is explored, and life in the Spirit ends in the hope that nothing can separate them from God's love.

structure.title: God's faithfulness and Israel
structure.summary: Paul grieves Israel's unbelief and argues that God's word has not failed. God's mercy is free, a remnant believes, Gentiles are grafted in, and all Israel will be saved.

structure.title: The life of a people shaped by mercy
structure.summary: Believers offer themselves to God, serve one another with their gifts, love their enemies, live under the governing authorities, and welcome one another across disputes about food and days.

structure.title: Paul's plans and greetings
structure.summary: Paul explains his mission, his coming trip to Jerusalem with the collection, and his hope to reach Spain, then greets many believers in Rome by name and closes with praise to God.

themes.title: The righteousness of God
themes.body: Paul's theme phrase has been read in several ways: as the righteous standing God gives to believers, as God's own saving faithfulness to his promises, or as both at once. The letter shows God as just in judging sin and just in justifying the one who believes (3:26). Whatever the precise emphasis, the phrase names God acting in Christ to set things right.

themes.title: Sin and death as powers
themes.body: Romans treats sin not only as wrong acts but as a power that reigns over humanity, entering through Adam and bringing death with it. That is why the answer cannot be simple self-improvement. People need to be rescued and brought under a new reign, the reign of grace.

themes.title: Faith and the law
themes.body: Paul insists that no one is justified by works of the law, yet he calls the law holy, righteous, and good. Faith does not nullify the law but upholds it. How to hold these together is one of the letter's great questions, and the key to much of the modern debate about Paul.

themes.title: Jew and Gentile together
themes.body: The gospel is for the Jew first and also for the Greek. God is not the God of Jews only, Abraham is the father of all who believe, and the church must welcome one another as Christ welcomed them. The unity of one people from many nations runs through the letter from its first chapter to its last.

themes.title: The Spirit and hope
themes.body: The Spirit gives life, bears witness that believers are God's children, helps them in weakness, and is the firstfruits of a coming redemption that will reach the whole groaning creation.

keyChapters.why: The letter's theme (1:16-17) and its opening account of humanity's refusal to honor God.
The verdict that all have sinned, and the central statement of righteousness through faith and Christ's atoning death (3:21-26).
Abraham as the pattern of justification by faith and the father of Jewish and Gentile believers alike.
Peace with God, and the comparison of Adam and Christ that frames the human story.
Union with Christ in his death and resurrection, and freedom from the reign of sin.
Life in the Spirit, adoption, the hope of creation, and the assurance that nothing can separate believers from God's love.
The start of Paul's wrestling with Israel's unbelief and God's freedom in mercy.
The turn to the life of a people shaped by mercy, beginning with bodies offered as living sacrifices.

parts.body:
Romans is a letter. Paul wrote it to the followers of Jesus in Rome, the capital of the Roman Empire, about twenty-five years after Jesus died and rose. It has 16 chapters. It is the longest of Paul's letters, and in the New Testament it comes first among them, straight after Acts.

When Paul wrote, he had never been to Rome. He hoped to visit on his way to Spain. So he wrote ahead, to introduce himself and the good news he preached, and to ask for the Roman believers' help and prayers.

The letter is an argument, laid out step by step. Paul states his theme near the start: “I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (1:16). ‘Gospel’ means good news. Then he works that sentence out. He shows what is wrong with the whole human race. He shows what God has done about it in Jesus, and how a person is set right with God as a gift received by trust. He describes the new life that follows. He asks whether God has kept his promises to Israel. And he shows how people saved by mercy should live together.

Few books have shaped the church more. Augustine, Martin Luther and John Wesley each came to a turning point while reading or hearing Romans, as the part on its history below tells.

Romans is not an easy book, and it is not meant to be read in pieces. Even the New Testament admits it: “Some parts of his letters are hard to understand” (2 Peter 3:16). But its questions are the deepest ones a person can ask: what is wrong with us, what has God done about it, and what kind of people does that make us?

The letter opens with its writer's name: “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle” (1:1). Almost every scholar, of every school, agrees that Paul wrote Romans. It is one of the letters of his that no serious study has doubted.

Paul was a Jew, “a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin” (11:1). Acts tells how he was trained as a Pharisee, a member of a strict group devoted to keeping God's law, and how he hunted down the first believers until the risen Jesus met him on the road to Damascus (Acts 9). After that he spent his life taking the good news to Gentiles, people who are not Jews. He wrote Romans after many years of that work.

Paul did not write the letter with his own hand. He spoke it, and another man wrote it down. Near the end that man adds his own line: “I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord” (16:22). Using a trained writer for a letter was common in the Roman world.

Who carried it to Rome? Paul begins his greetings with a woman: “I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea” (16:1). Cenchrea was the eastern port of Corinth. Paul asks the Romans to welcome her and help her, “For she has been a great help to many people, including me” (16:2). The word behind ‘great help’ was used of patrons, people of means who supported others. The letter does not say Phoebe carried it. But a letter like this one usually introduced the person who brought it, so most readers think she very likely did.

The word ‘servant’ in 16:1 is the Greek diakonos. It can mean a servant or helper in general, and it is also the word for the church office of deacon. Readers differ on which Paul means here.

Scholars do discuss the letter's form. In old manuscripts the closing words of praise (16:25-27) stand in different places, and some have argued that chapter 16, with its many names, was first a separate note. Most today hold that chapter 16 belongs to the letter to Rome.

parts.h: When and where it was written
parts.body:
Most scholars date Romans to about AD 57, give or take a year or two, and think Paul wrote it at Corinth in Greece. The clues fit together well.

Paul says he is about to take money to Jerusalem: “For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem” (15:26). Macedonia and Achaia were the Roman provinces of northern and southern Greece. This gift, which Paul gathered from his Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, also appears in his letters to Corinth. Acts says that near the end of this stage of his work Paul spent three months in Greece before setting out for Jerusalem (Acts 20:2-3).

The greetings point to Corinth too. Phoebe served the church at Cenchrea, Corinth's port (16:1). Paul sends greetings from “Gaius, who has hosted me and all the church” (16:23), very likely the Gaius whom Paul baptized at Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14). He also sends greetings from Erastus, “the city treasurer” (16:23). A stone with the name Erastus was found at Corinth in 1929, but whether it names the same man is disputed.

So the letter was written in a pause between two great tasks. Behind Paul lay years of work around the eastern Mediterranean. Ahead lay Jerusalem, where he feared trouble (15:31), and then, he hoped, Rome and Spain.

Things did not go as he planned. Acts tells that Paul was arrested in Jerusalem (Acts 21) and held for two years at Caesarea. When at last he reached Rome, about three years after writing this letter, he came as a prisoner under guard (Acts 28). The church there had already had his letter in its hands for years.

Rome was the greatest city of the empire, full of people from every province. It had a large Jewish community, with a number of synagogues, the meeting houses where Jews gathered to pray and to hear the Scriptures read.

No one knows who first brought the good news to Rome. Paul did not. He says he has not yet visited (1:13), and that he tries not to build “on someone else’s foundation” (15:20). Most likely Jewish believers who travelled to and from Rome carried it there early. Acts names visitors from Rome among the crowd at Pentecost (Acts 2:10).

The believers did not meet in a church building. There were none yet. They met in homes. Paul greets “the church that meets at their house” (16:5), the house of Prisca and Aquila. Other greetings seem to name other groups: “the brothers with them” (16:14) and “all the saints with them” (16:15). So many readers think Paul was writing to several small house churches across the city, not one large gathering.

The names in chapter 16 tell a story of their own. Some are Jewish: Paul calls Andronicus, Junia and Herodion his ‘fellow countrymen’ (16:7, 11). Others are Greek or Latin. Several are women. Some, like those ‘who belong to the household of Aristobulus’ (16:10), may have been slaves or freed slaves who belonged to a great house. The Roman church was mixed: Jew and Gentile, women and men, slave and free.

One event may help explain the letter. The Roman writer Suetonius says the emperor Claudius drove the Jews out of Rome because of disturbances stirred up by one ‘Chrestus’. Most scholars think this is a garbled form of ‘Christus’, Christ, and that the quarrels were over Jesus. Acts mentions the same expulsion: Aquila and Priscilla had come to Corinth because Claudius had ordered the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2). The usual date, about AD 49, comes from a later writer and is disputed.

Many scholars build on this a likely picture, though it is a reconstruction and not something the letter says. Jewish believers had to leave. For some years the house churches were led mostly by Gentiles. After Claudius died in AD 54, Jews could return, and Prisca and Aquila were back in Rome (16:3). Churches that had grown in a Gentile direction now had to welcome back Jewish believers with their own convictions about food and holy days. If this is right, it would help explain why Paul says so much about Jew and Gentile together, and why he pleads in chapters 14 and 15, “Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you” (15:7).

Paul gives some of his reasons himself.

He had long wanted to come to Rome. He prays to come at last (1:10), and he is eager to preach the gospel there too (1:15).

He was about to go to Jerusalem with the gift from his churches, and he was anxious. He asks the Romans to pray that he will be rescued from unbelievers in Judea, and that the believers in Jerusalem will accept the gift (15:30-31). The gift mattered to him because it showed that Gentile and Jewish believers belonged to one family.

After Jerusalem he planned to go west: “I hope to see you on my way to Spain” (15:24). He hoped the Roman churches would help send him. A church that was going to stand behind him needed to know what he preached.

And some people were saying hard things about his message. Paul mentions a charge that he taught, “Let us do evil that good may result” (3:8). Twice he asks whether grace means we can go on sinning (6:1, 6:15). So part of the letter answers those who thought his gospel of grace made the law worthless and made sin cheap.

Scholars weigh these reasons differently. Some read Romans mainly as a careful summary of Paul's gospel, written at a turning point in his work. Others stress that it speaks to a real, divided church, where Jewish and Gentile believers needed to hear that God's mercy had made them one people. Others stress the trip to Spain, or the gift for Jerusalem. Most see more than one aim at work, and the letter is richer for it.

Romans moves in large blocks. Seeing them helps a reader keep the thread.

Greeting and theme (1:1-17). Paul introduces himself and the gospel, which God “promised beforehand through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures” (1:2). Then he states the theme: the gospel is God's power to save everyone who believes, because in it the righteousness of God is revealed. And he quotes the prophet Habakkuk: “The righteous will live by faith” (1:17).

What is wrong (1:18 to 3:20). The whole human race has turned from God. Gentiles who did not have the law turned to idols. Jews who had the law did not keep it. Paul ends: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (3:23), and no one will be set right with God by keeping the law.

What God has done (3:21 to 5:21). “But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed” (3:21). God sets people right with himself freely, by grace, through Jesus's death, and they receive it by faith. Abraham was set right with God in just this way, before he was circumcised (chapter 4). The result is peace with God, and a new head for humanity: Adam brought sin and death, and Christ brings grace and life (chapter 5).

The new life (chapters 6 to 8). Grace does not mean going on in sin. Believers have died with Christ and live a new life (chapter 6). The law is good but cannot free a person from sin (chapter 7). The Spirit gives life, makes believers God's children, and holds them in a love nothing can break (chapter 8).

God and Israel (chapters 9 to 11). If most of Israel has not believed, has God's word failed? Paul grieves for his people and argues that it has not: God's mercy is free, a remnant believes, Gentiles are grafted in, and “all Israel will be saved” (11:26).

The life that follows (12:1 to 15:13). “Therefore”, in view of God's mercy, believers offer their whole lives to God. They serve each other, love their enemies, live under the governing authorities, and welcome one another across their quarrels over food and days.

Plans and greetings (15:14 to 16:27). Paul's travel plans, a long list of names, and praise to God.

Romans quotes the Old Testament more often than any other letter of Paul. Paul's point is that the gospel is not a new religion. It is what God promised long before, “attested by the Law and the Prophets” (3:21). He even says, “everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction” (15:4). Three passages carry special weight.

The first is Habakkuk 2:4. Habakkuk was a prophet in Judah shortly before the Babylonians conquered it. He complained that God was slow to act against evil. God told him to wait, because the answer would come at its set time. Then came the line: “the righteous will live by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4). The Hebrew word behind ‘faith’ there means steadiness or faithfulness. In Habakkuk it described the person who keeps trusting God when the promise is delayed. Paul makes the line the banner of his whole letter (1:17). For Paul, the one who trusts God, not the one who earns standing, is the one God counts righteous and who truly lives.

The second is Abraham. Genesis says, “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). Paul quotes it in Romans 4 and points out when it happened: before Abraham was circumcised. So Abraham is the father of all who trust God, Jews and Gentiles alike.

The third is Adam. Genesis 2 and 3 tell how the first man disobeyed God and death followed. In Romans 5 Paul sets Adam beside Christ. One man's disobedience brought sin and death to all. One man's obedience brings grace and life.

There are many more. In chapter 3 Paul strings together lines from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that no one is righteous. In chapters 9 to 11 he quotes Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Hosea and Isaiah again and again as he wrestles with Israel's unbelief. In chapter 15 he gathers verses from the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms about the nations praising God. The notes on each chapter name every quotation and say what it meant in its own place.

Paul also quotes the Greek translation of the Old Testament, called the Septuagint, which his Greek-speaking hearers knew. So his wording sometimes differs a little from an English Bible translated from the Hebrew.

Romans uses a few words again and again. Knowing them makes the letter much easier to follow.

Faith (Greek pistis) means trust: relying on God and on what he has promised. It is not a feeling, and it is not a good deed that earns a reward. It is how a person receives what God gives. The same Greek word can also mean faithfulness, which matters for one debate set out below.

Grace (Greek charis) means a gift given freely, to someone who has not earned it. In Paul's world the word was used of the favour of a patron. Paul uses it of God's undeserved kindness in Christ: we “are justified freely by His grace” (3:24).

Law (Greek nomos) usually means the law God gave Israel through Moses, the commandments of the first five books of the Bible. Paul calls it “holy” and its commands “holy, righteous, and good” (7:12). His point is that it cannot make a person right with God or set him free from sin. Sometimes Paul uses ‘law’ in a looser sense, of a rule or a power at work (7:23, 8:2).

Flesh (Greek sarx) can mean simply the body, or human descent: Jesus was descended from David “according to the flesh” (1:3). But often Paul uses it for human nature turned away from God, weak and bent toward sin. To live ‘according to the flesh’ is to live as if God were not there.

Sin (Greek hamartia) is more than wrong acts. In Romans sin is pictured as a power, almost a master, that rules people and pays its wages in death (6:23). That is why people need rescue, not just better effort.

The Spirit (Greek pneuma) is God's Holy Spirit. Romans 8 names the Spirit more than any other chapter in the letter. The Spirit gives life, leads God's children, prays for them in their weakness, and is the first share of what is still to come.

Two more words, ‘righteousness’ and ‘justified’, need parts of their own, because Christians understand them in different ways.

In English, ‘righteous’ and ‘justify’ look like two different words. In Greek they are one family: dikaios, righteous or just; dikaiosynē, righteousness or justice; dikaioō, to justify. All of them are about being in the right.

The verb comes from the law court. When a judge justified someone, he declared that person in the right, not guilty. So ‘justified’ in Romans means set right with God, declared in the right before him. Paul's great surprise is that God does this for the guilty: Abraham believed “in Him who justifies the wicked” (4:5). The question Paul faces is how God can do that and still be a just judge. His answer is the cross (3:25-26).

‘The righteousness of God’ (1:17, 3:21) is read in more than one way. Some read it as the right standing God gives to those who believe. Others read it as God's own faithfulness, his saving action to keep his promises and put the world right. Many think Paul means both: God, faithful to his promises, acts in Christ to set people right with himself.

How exactly does this happen? Here the churches differ, and the differences are real and old.

Lutheran and Reformed churches, following Martin Luther and John Calvin, teach that God declares the sinner righteous for Christ's sake. Christ's righteousness is credited to the believer's account as a gift, received by faith alone. A real change of life always follows, but it is not the reason God accepts the sinner.

The Catholic Church teaches, in words its Catechism takes from the Council of Trent, that justification ‘is not only the remission of sins, but also the sanctification and renewal of the interior man’. God's verdict and God's real change inside a person belong together. Grace comes first and is never earned.

The Orthodox churches confess that salvation is wholly God's gift in Christ. But they do not make the law court the main picture. They speak of salvation as union with God and sharing in his life by grace, and they see justification as one true picture among many, not to be cut off from the healing of the whole person in the life of the church.

In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification. They agreed on basic truths and named the differences that remain.

These notes do not choose between these teachings. All of them agree that sinners are set right with God by his grace, through Christ, and not by their own deeds.

Paul says, “For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (3:28). What are ‘works of the law’? Christians and scholars read the phrase in two main ways.

The traditional reading, long taught in Protestant churches, takes ‘works of the law’ to mean everything a person does to obey God's law, done as a way to stand right with God. On this reading Paul's target is any attempt to earn God's favour. No one keeps the law well enough, so no one can stand on his own record. Romans 4 seems to say just this: to the worker, wages are paid as a debt, but God credits righteousness to the one who trusts him “who justifies the wicked” (4:5).

A second reading is often called the ‘new perspective’ on Paul. In 1977 the scholar E. P. Sanders published Paul and Palestinian Judaism. He argued that the Judaism of Paul's day was not a religion of earning salvation. God chose Israel by grace first, and the law was the way to stay faithful within that covenant. Sanders called this pattern ‘covenantal nomism’, from nomos, law. In 1982 James Dunn gave a lecture called ‘The New Perspective on Paul’, which named the approach, and N. T. Wright and others developed it.

On this reading, ‘works of the law’ means above all the practices that marked Jews off from other peoples: circumcision, the food laws, and the Sabbath. Paul's point is that Gentiles do not have to become Jews to belong to God's people. Paul asks, “Is God the God of Jews only? Is He not the God of Gentiles too?” (3:29). Justification, on this view, is about sin and also about who belongs to God's one family.

Each reading has strong defenders. Those who hold the second say it recovers Paul's concern for Jew and Gentile at one table. Their critics answer that it weakens Paul's teaching that grace excludes every kind of human achievement. Many readers take something from both: Paul did fight the idea that Gentiles must become Jews, and he also said that no one can boast before God at all (3:27). These notes set out both readings and do not settle the question.

parts.h: ‘Faith in Christ’, or ‘the faithfulness of Christ’?
parts.body:
A few times in his letters Paul uses a short Greek phrase, pistis Christou. Word for word it says ‘faith of Christ’. It comes in Romans 3:22 and 3:26, in Galatians 2:16, and in Philippians 3:9.

The Greek can be read two ways. It can mean faith in Christ: our trust, placed in him. Most English Bibles read it so, and the BSB says that this righteousness “comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe” (3:22). Or it can mean Christ's own faith, his faithfulness: Jesus's trust in his Father and his obedience all the way to the cross. A few translations read it that way.

Those who prefer ‘faithfulness of Christ’ point out that 3:22 would otherwise say the same thing twice, ‘through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe’. They see in the phrase Jesus's own faithful obedience, which Paul names in 5:19. The American scholar Richard Hays argued for this reading in The Faith of Jesus Christ (1983), and many have followed him.

Those who prefer ‘faith in Christ’ answer that Paul repeats himself for emphasis, that Romans 4 is all about Abraham's trust as the pattern for ours, and some argue that the early church writers mostly read the phrase this way. Many scholars still hold the traditional reading.

This is a question about grammar, and good scholars disagree. It does not change the heart of the gospel. On either reading, Paul teaches both things elsewhere: Christ was faithful and obedient for us, and we are to trust him. These notes do not choose.

Romans has stood at the turning points of many lives, and of the church itself.

In 386 Augustine, a brilliant teacher who had long resisted the faith, sat in a garden in Milan in deep distress. In his Confessions he tells how he heard a child's voice repeating, as he understood it, ‘take up and read’. He opened Paul's letters and read the first lines his eyes fell on, Romans 13:13-14, about putting off drunkenness and sexual sin and clothing oneself with the Lord Jesus Christ. He became a Christian, and later one of the most influential teachers the church has had.

Martin Luther, a friar (a member of a religious order) and a teacher of the Bible at Wittenberg in Germany, lectured on Romans in 1515 and 1516. In 1545, near the end of his life, he looked back on the change in his understanding. He had hated the phrase ‘the righteousness of God’ in Romans 1:17, because he took it as the justice by which God punishes sinners. Then he came to see it as the righteousness God gives, by which the righteous live by faith. Historians still debate exactly when this happened. That reading of Romans stood at the centre of the Protestant Reformation.

On 24 May 1738, in London, John Wesley went to a meeting in Aldersgate Street where someone was reading Luther's preface to the letter to the Romans. Wesley wrote in his journal, ‘I felt my heart strangely warmed’. The Methodist movement grew from his preaching in the years that followed.

Karl Barth, a young Swiss pastor, wrote a commentary on Romans during the First World War. It came out at the end of 1918, dated 1919, and he rewrote it completely for a second edition in 1922. It drew strong supporters and strong critics, and it led to his being made a professor at Göttingen in 1921.

In 1977 E. P. Sanders's Paul and Palestinian Judaism began the long debate about Paul and the Judaism of his day, set out above. And in 1999 Catholics and Lutherans signed their Joint Declaration on what Romans means by ‘justified’.

Each of these readers found something different in Romans. All of them found that it would not leave them as they were.

Romans is often read in ways that make it smaller than it is.

It is not only a private road to heaven. Romans does tell each person how to be right with God, and that matters deeply. But Paul's larger question is about God himself: is God faithful to what he promised Israel, and to his plan to bless all nations through Abraham? The letter is about one people from many nations, and about a whole creation waiting to be set free (8:21).

It is not against the Jewish people. In chapters 9 to 11 Paul grieves for his own people: “I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” (9:2). He insists that God has not rejected them (11:1), that “God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (11:29), and he warns Gentile believers not to be proud (11:18-20). When Paul presses hard questions on Jewish readers in chapter 2, he speaks as a Jew to fellow Jews, in the manner of Israel's prophets. For centuries some Christians used words from the New Testament to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. Romans itself forbids it.

It is not a political program. Romans 13:1-7 tells believers to submit to the governing authorities, and Christians have long debated what that means when rulers do wrong. But the passage sits inside a call to love: bless those who persecute you, repay no one evil for evil, overcome evil with good (12:14-21). Romans does not tell anyone which party or ruler to support, and these notes do not either.

It is not a set of separate verses to be pulled out one by one. Many famous verses, such as 3:23, 6:23 and 8:28, mean more inside their paragraph than on their own. Romans is an argument. It is best read as one.

Read it aloud. Romans was written to be read aloud to gatherings of believers, most of whom did not have a copy of their own. Hearing it helps the argument carry.

Read it whole, or in large sections, before stopping on single verses. A first reading in one or two sittings shows the shape that this page describes.

Follow the word ‘therefore’. It marks the hinges of the letter: “Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God” (5:1); “Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (8:1); “Therefore I urge you, brothers” (12:1). Each time, ask what it is there for.

Listen for the questions. Paul often raises an objection in the voice of an imagined critic and then answers it, a style ancient teachers used. Questions like “What then shall we say?” (6:1) mark a turn in the argument, and his answer is often a sharp ‘By no means’ or ‘Certainly not’.

Look up the Old Testament quotations in their own places. Paul chose them with care, and their setting often adds to his point.

Do not skip chapter 16. Its long list of names shows the real people who first heard the letter: women and men, Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, meeting in homes.

And read it with others if you can. It was written to churches, not to a lone reader. Its last chapters show that its doctrine was meant to make people who had been divided into one family.

hard.line: ‘The wrath of God’. What Paul means by it, said plainly: God handing people over to what they have chosen. And what can be known of God from the world he made.
Same-sex relations in 1:26-27. What Paul says, how Christians read it, and why the very next verse turns the charge on anyone who judges.
Gentiles who ‘do by nature what the law requires’. Who are they, and what does it say about those who never heard?
‘The atoning sacrifice’. Propitiation, expiation or mercy seat, and how Christians understand what the cross did.
Sin and death through one man. Original sin in the Western and Eastern churches, a question of translation, and Adam and human origins.
‘I do not do what I want to do’. Is the ‘I’ a believer, a person before faith, or Israel or Adam speaking? Three readings.
‘All things work together for good’. What the verse promises and what it does not, and how churches read ‘predestined’.
‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’. What the words meant in Malachi, and whether Paul speaks of persons or of peoples.
God has mercy on whom he wants, and hardens whom he wants. The potter and the clay, and how Reformed and Arminian readers take it.
‘And so all Israel will be saved’. Who is ‘all Israel’, and when? The main readings, with no claim about any modern state.
‘Submit to the governing authorities’. What it asks, what it does not, and how Christians have read it under unjust rulers.
Andronicus and Junia, ‘outstanding among the apostles’. Junia as a woman, and what the phrase and the word ‘apostle’ may mean.

words.line: Greek euangelion, good news. For Paul, the news about God's Son, promised beforehand in the Scriptures (1:1-4), which is God's power to save everyone who believes (1:16).
Greek dikaiosynē, being in the right. ‘The righteousness of God’ (1:17) may mean the right standing God gives, God's own saving faithfulness, or both.
Greek dikaioō, a law-court word: to declare someone in the right. God ‘justifies the wicked’ who trust him (4:5). Churches differ on what more it includes.
Greek pistis, trust in God and his promise. The same word can mean faithfulness. Abraham is Paul's great example (4:3, 4:20-21).
Greek charis, a free gift to someone who has not earned it. ‘Justified freely by His grace’ (3:24).
Greek nomos. Usually the law God gave Israel through Moses: holy and good (7:12), but unable to set a person right with God or free from sin (3:20, 8:3).
Deeds done in obedience to the law of Moses (3:20, 3:28). Read as any effort to earn standing with God, or above all as the marks of being Jewish, such as circumcision.
Greek sarx. The body or human descent (1:3), but often human nature turned from God and weak against sin (8:5-8).
Greek hamartia. Wrong acts, and also a power that rules people like a master and pays its wages in death (6:23).
Greek pneuma. God's Holy Spirit, who gives life, makes believers God's children, and helps them in weakness (8:11, 8:15, 8:26).
Greek hilastērion (3:25), the BSB's ‘atoning sacrifice’, with ‘propitiation’ in its footnote. In the Greek Old Testament the same word names the mercy seat on the ark.
Greek apolutrōsis, setting free by paying a price, as a slave or prisoner was freed. Believers are justified ‘through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus’ (3:24).
Greek huiothesia, being made a son and heir. By the Spirit every believer, woman or man, is God's child and heir (8:15-17).
Greek ethnē, the nations: everyone who is not Jewish. Paul was sent to bring them to faith (1:5), and Romans shows Jew and Gentile made one people (3:29-30).

timeline.what: Claudius is emperor. Acts names him for sending the Jews out of Rome (Acts 18:2).
Claudius expels Jews from Rome, Suetonius says because of disturbances over ‘Chrestus’. Aquila and Priscilla come to Corinth (Acts 18:2). The year comes from a later writer.
Gallio is governor of Achaia, as an inscription at Delphi shows. Paul is in Corinth for the first time, with Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18).
Nero is emperor. After Claudius's death Jews can return to Rome, and Prisca and Aquila are back there when Paul writes (16:3).
Paul writes Romans, most likely at Corinth, during three months in Greece (Acts 20:2-3), before taking the gift from his churches to Jerusalem (15:25-26).
Paul is arrested in Jerusalem (Acts 21) and held for two years at Caesarea, as he had feared (15:31).
Paul reaches Rome at last, as a prisoner, and stays two years under guard, receiving all who come to him (Acts 28:30).
The great fire of Rome. Nero blames the Christians, and many are killed, as the Roman historian Tacitus reports.
In a garden in Milan, Augustine reads Romans 13:13-14 and becomes a Christian, as he tells in his Confessions.
Martin Luther lectures on Romans at Wittenberg. In 1545 he tells how Romans 1:17 opened to him.
At a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, John Wesley hears Luther's preface to Romans read and feels his ‘heart strangely warmed’.
Karl Barth's commentary on Romans appears (printed at the end of 1918), rewritten in a second edition in 1922.
E. P. Sanders publishes Paul and Palestinian Judaism. In 1982 James Dunn names the ‘new perspective on Paul’.
The Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation sign a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification.

places.name: Corinth
places.line: Where Paul most likely wrote the letter, in the house of Gaius (16:23). Phoebe served the church at Cenchrea, Corinth's eastern port (16:1).

places.name: Rome
places.line: The capital of the empire, where the letter went: to house churches Paul had not founded and had never visited (1:13), meeting in homes (16:5).

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Where Paul was about to take the gift from Macedonia and Achaia for the poor believers (15:25-26). He asks the Romans to pray for his safety there (15:31).

teaching.mapNote: The letter was written at Corinth and sent to Rome, while Paul was about to sail for Jerusalem. Spain, where he hoped to go next (15:24, 15:28), lies far to the west, beyond the edge of this map. Illyricum (15:19), the Roman province along the east shore of the Adriatic Sea, lies mostly beyond its top edge.
